title: Operator overloading (custom operators for your types)
hook: Operators like `+` and `==` are just static methods with special syntax. You can define them for your own types — but only when the type is a natural fit, like money or coordinates.

blocks.text: **Operator overloading** lets you define what `+`, `-`, `==`, and other operators mean for your types. Under the hood, they are `public static` methods named `operator +`, `operator ==`, etc. C# 14 added **user-defined compound assignment** (`+=`, `-=`) so mutable value types can update in place instead of going through `x = x + y`.

entries.plainDefinition: Defining custom behavior for operators on your own types via static methods.
entries.example: `public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b)`

entries.plainDefinition: A custom `operator +=` that mutates in place instead of creating a copy through `x = x + y`.
An implicit or explicit cast between your type and another. Easy to make surprising.
entries.example: `public static implicit operator string(Token t) => t.Value;`

entries.plainDefinition: Overloading `==` and `!=`. Must be paired with `Equals` and `GetHashCode` (module 05).
entries.example: `public static bool operator ==(Money a, Money b) => a.Amount == b.Amount;`

blocks.text: Well-designed operators make value types feel natural — adding two `Money` amounts or comparing two `DateRange` values. Poorly designed operators hide allocation, parsing failures, or incorrect equality. Overload operators on value-like types with clear semantics, not on service classes or workers.

blocks.title: Pair == with Equals and GetHashCode
blocks.body: Overloading `==` without consistent `Equals` and `GetHashCode` breaks dictionaries and sets. Full equality design is module 05.

items.title: Operators are public static methods
items.body: Named `operator +`, `operator ==`, etc. At least one parameter must be your type.

items.title: Overload on value-like types
items.body: Money, coordinates, time spans, cache key composition — yes. Worker classes — no.

items.title: Pair equality operators with Equals/GetHashCode
items.body: If you overload `==`, override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` consistently.

items.title: C# 14 compound assignment for in-place update
items.body: Use `operator +=` on mutable value types where in-place update is the contract. Skip it on immutable records.

diagram.title: Operator overload decision
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  Q[Should I overload?] --> V{Value-like type with clear math?}
  V -->|yes| OK[Define operator methods]
  V -->|no| NO[Use named methods instead]
  OK --> EQ{Overloading ==?}
  EQ -->|yes| GH[Also override Equals + GetHashCode]
  EQ -->|no| DONE[Done]

snippet.label: Immutable Money with operator +
snippet.explanation: Line 6: `operator +` is a static method with special syntax. Line 12: returns a new immutable value. Line 15: callers write natural `+` syntax.

snippet.label: C# 14 compound assignment on a mutable struct
snippet.explanation: Line 5: C# 14 user-defined `+=` mutates in place. Without it, `total += 10` would rewrite as `total = total + 10`, copying the struct twice.

snippet.label: What NOT to overload
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–3: implicit conversion from `string` would throw or allocate unexpectedly. Lines 10–16: `TryCreate` makes failure explicit — the pattern interviewers prefer.

blocks.title: Operators in C# vs JS/TS
rows: Always `x = x + y` semantics for objects
JS `==` coercion; TS has no operator overloading

blocks.title: Overloading == without GetHashCode
blocks.body: A class with custom `==` but default `GetHashCode` will break `Dictionary` and `HashSet` lookups. Module 05 covers the full equality contract.

blocks.title: Implicit conversions that throw or allocate
blocks.body: An implicit `string` to `Token` conversion hides parsing failures and allocations. Use named factory methods like `TryCreate` instead.

interviewTakeaways: Operators are static methods; keep them on value-like types.
C# 14 compound assignment can avoid the `x = x + y` copy on mutable structs.
commonPitfalls: Overloading `==` on a class and forgetting `GetHashCode`.
Implicit conversions that throw or allocate in surprising places.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript does not let you overload `+` for a class in a first-class way beyond `valueOf` hacks. C# operators are real metadata methods.
TypeScript cannot add operators to types. You write `add(a, b)` functions. C# can make `+` a named static method.
